title: Pre-Listing Renovations in Winnipeg: What to Fix Before You Sell
metaTitle: Pre-Listing Renovations in Winnipeg: What to Fix First
metaDescription: Selling in Winnipeg? See which pre-listing renovations buyers notice, what inspectors flag, and what to skip before you list your home.
excerpt: Selling in Winnipeg? See which pre-listing renovations buyers notice, what inspectors flag, and what to skip before you list your home.
answer: Fix what an inspector would write up first, then what buyers see in photos: fresh neutral paint, worn flooring, small kitchen and bathroom updates, a tired front door or failed window seals, and the entry. Skip major remodels and bold finishes, and make sure any work that needs a permit has one.

blocks.x: Winnipeg sellers have more competition than they did a year ago. The Winnipeg Regional Real Estate Board's [September 2026 results](/blog/winnipeg-housing-market-september-2026) showed softer sales and more active listings, especially detached homes, even as the year-to-date detached average hit a record. That makes pre-listing renovations in Winnipeg a question of priorities: which to do first, and which to skip.
More choice means buyers can be picky. The homes that stand out are the ones with no obvious projects.
Why buyers punish visible problems
Many buyers subtract the cost of every project they see from their offer, and they may guess high. A worn floor, a dated bathroom or peeling exterior paint can cost a seller in negotiation.
With more listings to choose from, some buyers simply skip homes that need work.
The pre-listing renovation priority list for Winnipeg sellers
Focus on what buyers see in photos and what inspectors flag.

**1. Fix anything an inspector will write up.** Leaky taps, cracked tile, sticking doors, missing handrails and damaged caulking. Fixing them before listing removes easy negotiating points. Foundation cracks in older homes on clay soil are different: a crack that is widening, offset or leaking needs a structural engineer's assessment first. See [basement cracks on clay soil](/blog/clay-soil-basement-cracks-winnipeg).

**2. Paint.** Fresh, neutral interior paint makes rooms look clean in photos and covers marks and wear. Touch up exterior trim and doors too, when the weather allows. Before anyone sands, note that a house built before 1960 probably has lead-based paint, [Health Canada](https://www.canada.ca/en/health-canada/services/home-safety/lead-based-paint.html) says, and it warns against removing that paint with sanders or heat guns.

**3. Flooring.** Replace visibly worn carpet or damaged [flooring](/services/flooring) in main living areas. Durable luxury vinyl plank photographs well and is a practical choice for busy family areas. Older floor tiles may contain asbestos, so [have them tested](/blog/asbestos-testing-before-renovating-manitoba) before anyone lifts them.

**4. Kitchen refresh, not a full remodel.** New cabinet hardware, lighting, faucet and possibly counters can update a kitchen without the cost and time of a [full kitchen renovation](/services/kitchen-renovations).
**5. Bathroom touch-ups.** Re-grout, re-caulk, swap the vanity light and mirror, and replace a stained toilet seat or dated fixtures.
**6. Windows and doors.** A tired front door or foggy, failed window seals stand out in listing photos and raise questions about heating costs.
**7. Curb appeal.** Clean the siding, repair masonry, and make sure the entry is lit and inviting, especially for fall and winter showings.
What not to do

**Don't start a major remodel** right before selling. Full kitchen and [bathroom renovations](/services/bathroom-renovations) or [basement developments](/services/basement-renovations) take time, and you may not get the full cost back at sale.
**Don't choose bold finishes.** Neutral colours and materials appeal to the most buyers.
**Don't skip permits.** Buyers can run [the City's free permit search](/blog/check-permit-history-winnipeg-house) on a Winnipeg address, and unpermitted work can delay or derail a sale.
Timing for a winter listing

Winter listings can face fewer buyers, and with more active listings than a year ago, you can't count on less competition. Interior paint, flooring and fixture updates can happen any time, so do those first.

Exterior painting and masonry need warmer weather. Once the cold sets in, [book that work for late spring](/blog/exterior-painting-winnipeg-when-to-paint). If you list before then, price the home to reflect any visible exterior wear.
The bottom line
In a market with more listings, move-in ready homes stand out. A short list of targeted renovations removes easy objections and can help protect your price.
